title: Montana’s Wolf Policy: Broad Killing, Narrow Benefits
author: John Carter
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/graywolf-680x439.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/18/montanas-
wolf-policy-broad-killing-narrow-benefits/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/graywolf-680x439.png)

Gray Wolf, Tracy Brooks, USFWS.

**_Science, public opinion, and the political economy of predator control_**

On August 19, the Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission will meet to decide the
fate of wolves in Montana. The proposal is to kill 250 wolves across the state
through hunting and trapping. Additionally, up to 15 “removals” on any
individual private property for threats to livestock, persons, or pets is
allowed. Apparently, there is no limit as to how many of these “properties”
can be included, thus no limit on wolves.

Then there is to be no limit on removals by MFWP, USDA Wildlife Services, or
others “in defense of property or human safety”. Thus, there is seemingly no
real limit to killing of wolves under the current proposal. While the public
comment period closed on August 12, there is an opportunity to register to
make additional comments at the August 19 public meeting via
[Zoom](https://fwp.mt.gov/aboutfwp/commission/august-2026-meeting). This is
available until August 18.

We submitted detailed
[comments](https://app.box.com/s/laje02xkytn1tfws7w8ctpuu7wmg0hk4) and
provided a [report](https://app.box.com/s/3nxip1ux5e6w2myjzoxgbhretqms73eg)
that analyzed Montana management of wolves in comparison to other states and
European countries. Montana does not rank very high, as it lacks a proven
method to document wolf populations and statistics and its models are highly
questionable in accuracy of prediction. While MFWP is working to improve,
wolves are needlessly being killed.

Montana’s wolf debate is often framed as a conflict between wolves and
livestock, but the state’s management system frequently applies a landscape-
wide remedy to a highly localized problem. Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks
(FWP) authorizes general hunting and trapping seasons across wolf range while
also conducting targeted removals after verified livestock depredations. Those
two tools are not equivalent. Hunting or trapping kills wolves largely
according to where hunters and trappers have access and success; targeted
control removes identified wolves or packs where a conflict occurred.

Montana’s own research provides a clear answer. A 2018 FWP-led study by
DeCesare and colleagues analyzed wolf-livestock conflicts from 2005 through
2015. Targeted management reduced recurrent depredations, but public harvest
did not reliably eliminate conflict from one year to the next. Even where
higher harvest was associated with fewer depredations, the authors estimated
the effect at 5.7 fewer depredation events statewide per year, an 8% reduction
from the average annual statewide total. The spatial mismatch was equally
important: the study reported that 83% of documented depredations occurred on
private land, while only 41% of public wolf harvest occurred there. The
authors concluded that removing relatively small numbers of wolves through
either partial pack control or public harvest may do little to prevent future
depredations in recurrent-conflict areas. We suggest that preventive measures
are the solution for livestock producers and feel it is past time for them to
do their part.

The economic scale of the interests surrounding this policy is also revealing.
According to the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) for 2024, Montana’s
hunting/shooting/trapping activity generated approximately $118.4 million in
value added in 2024, while guiding and outfitting contributed $162.5 million.
Dividing these figures by Montana’s $78.4 billion 2024 GDP gives 0.15% for
hunting/shooting/trapping and 0.21% for guiding and outfitting. A separate
2026 University of Montana Institute for Tourism & Recreation Research study
found that fishing generated the most outfitting revenue, followed by wildlife
viewing and then hunting. Guided hunting is consequently only one component of
the broader outfitting economy. These sectors are not bulwarks of Montana’s
economy. The hunting and trapping of wolves is even smaller as a subset of the
overall recreation or hunting/trapping/shooting sector and its absence would
hardly be missed in Montana’s economy.

In a 2023 survey of Montana residents by the University of Montana in
cooperation with FWP, 74% of the general population said they were tolerant or
very tolerant of wolves on the landscape. The survey also found that 58% of
the general population was tolerant or very tolerant of wolf hunting, down
from 71% in 2012. Support for trapping was lower and declining. Wolves were
delisted in Montana in 2011. The recent 16th-annual Conservation in the West
poll shows high concern among voters about such rollback of environmental
protection laws. On a partisan breakdown, 94% of Democrats, 87% of
Independents, and 74% of Republicans in Montana have serious problems with the
rollback of environmental protections.

Hunting and outfitting have a disproportionate role in decisions about
wildlife management under the North American model where selling licenses to
hunt and fish provide revenue to Game and Fish departments; thus, a conflict
exists where the general public’s preferences for wildlife and habitat
protection are subordinate to the desires of the department and those who fund
the department. Likewise, the other factor in killing wolves is the livestock
industry, whose political influence in western states is clear, while their
economic value is minimal compared to overall agriculture. Public lands
ranching is insignificant, while costing taxpayers to subsidize it.

BEA reports that Montana’s real GDP from farms—crop and animal production
combined—was $1.43 billion in 2024. Comparing this to the GDP for the same
year gives approximately 1.8%. Because the farm series includes both crop and
animal production, livestock alone necessarily accounts for less than the full
farm-sector percentage. Claims that wolf policy protects a large fraction of
Montana’s entire economy therefore overstate the direct economic exposure,
even though wolf losses can be important to individual livestock producers.

The disparity is greater for federal public-land grazing. Economist Thomas
Michael Power, whose analysis was summarized in a published article in the
Arkansas National Agricultural Law Center 1998), concluded that western
ranching’s political visibility exceeded its measurable role in modern state
economies. At the time, for Montana, the published summary reported 1,085 jobs
associated with federal grazing, equal to 0.25% of statewide employment, and
0.14% of statewide income. While these are historical data, the implication
remains valid. It’s minuscule.

A more recent American Farm Bureau Federation analysis estimates the value of
livestock sales attributable to forage consumed on public lands. It reports
that Montana is among the western states with more than $100 million annually
in livestock sales attributable to public-land forage. Using $100 million only
as an order-of-magnitude comparison against Montana’s $78.4 billion 2024 GDP
produces approximately 0.13%. This doesn’t account for the huge subsidies
ranchers receive from the public’s taxes.

These numbers do not make hunting, outfitting, or ranching unimportant; they
show that political influence is not necessarily proportional to GDP. These
are organized constituencies that repeatedly participate in legislative,
commission, and agency processes. By contrast, the 74% of surveyed general-
population respondents who expressed tolerance or high tolerance for wolves
represent a much more diffuse but much larger public interest.

A defensible wolf policy should therefore separate livestock protection from
generalized predator reduction. Where wolves repeatedly depredate livestock,
FWP should verify the conflict, require reasonable preventive measures, and
then use targeted removal when necessary. Where no conflict exists, killing
wolves should not be justified as livestock protection without evidence that
the action is likely to significantly reduce depredation. Montana’s own
research shows why: conflict is geographically concentrated, while public
harvest is not. Broad killing may reduce wolf numbers, but reduction in
numbers is not the same thing as reduction in conflict.

The management standard should be simple: use the least generalized lethal
tool capable of accomplishing a defined biological or conflict-management
objective. That would preserve authority for decisive action against
demonstrably problem wolves while reducing unnecessary killing of stable packs
elsewhere. It would also align policy more closely with what Montana’s
science, economy, and public opinion actually show—a state in which wolves are
broadly accepted, livestock conflicts are real but localized, and the
industries most vocal in wolf policy represent far smaller shares of the
overall economy than their political visibility implies.

Wolves selectively prey on vulnerable animals and may, under certain
conditions, reduce or delay modeled chronic wasting disease outbreaks. Wolves
and other carnivores nevertheless influence elk abundance, distribution,
aggregation, carrion availability, and scavenger communities, all of which can
affect disease transmission. Montana research also indicates that diverse
scavenger communities can shorten the persistence of potentially infectious
reproductive material. These ecological functions should be considered
alongside livestock conflicts and harvest objectives rather than treated as
separate issues.

We at Yellowstone to Uintas Connection value predators and scavengers for
their role in the ecosystem and their own being. We oppose the killing of
predators in general and particularly on public lands where ecosystems should
function naturally and livestock producers should live with the consequences
of placing their livestock on our public lands and national forests.
